title: Ἁλιεὺς ⟨ὕδωρ τύπτων⟩
titleEn: The Fisherman Who Beat the Water
part: The Fisherman Who Beat the Water (Chambry 27 · Perry 26)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 27 (= Perry 26). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: A fisherman was fishing in a certain river.
sentences.n: The imperfect ἡλίευε sets the scene rather than reporting an event: he was at his fishing when the story opens.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ κατατείνας τὰ δίκτυα, ὡς ἐμπεριέλαβεν ἑκατέρωθεν τὸ ῥεῦμα, προσδήσας κάλῳ λινῷ λίθον, ἔτυπτε τὸ ὕδωρ, ὅπως οἱ ἰχθύες φεύγοντες ἀπροφυλάκτως τοῖς βρόχοις ἐμπέσωσι.
sentences.tr: Kai dē katateinas ta diktya, hōs emperielaben hekaterōthen to rheuma, prosdēsas kalōi linōi lithon, etypte to hydōr, hopōs hoi ichthyes pheugontes aprophylaktōs tois brochois empesōsi.
sentences.l: And so, having stretched his nets across, when he had enclosed the current on either side, having tied a stone to a flaxen rope, he beat the water, so that the fish, fleeing, might fall unguardedly into the meshes.
sentences.i: So he stretched his nets across, and when he had shut in the current on either side, he tied a stone to a flaxen cord and beat the water, so that the fish, fleeing, might rush unawares into the nets.
sentences.n: καὶ δή, “and so, and in fact,” moves the narrative on a step. Another aorist-participle chain (κατατείνας … προσδήσας) around one imperfect main verb, ἔτυπτε, “he kept beating.” ὅπως with the aorist subjunctive (ἐμπέσωσι) is a purpose clause. βρόχος is a noose or mesh; κάλως is properly a ship's rope, here one of flax. The trick described is real fishing practice, not invention.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ περὶ τὸν τόπον οἰκούντων τις θεασάμενος αὐτὸν τοῦτο ποιοῦντα, ἐμέμφετο ἐπὶ τῷ τὸν ποταμὸν θολοῦν καὶ μὴ ἐᾶν αὐτοὺς διαυγὲς ὕδωρ πίνειν.
sentences.tr: Tōn de peri ton topon oikountōn tis theasamenos auton touto poiounta, emempheto epi tōi ton potamon tholoun kai mē ean autous diauges hydōr pinein.
sentences.l: But one of those dwelling around the place, having seen him doing this, found fault with him for the muddying of the river and the not allowing them to drink clear water.
sentences.i: But one of the people living thereabouts saw him at it and reproached him for muddying the river and leaving them no clear water to drink.
sentences.n: τῶν … οἰκούντων τις, “one of those dwelling…”: an articular participle used as a noun, with the partitive genitive standing before τις. θεασάμενος αὐτὸν … ποιοῦντα is the regular way to say “saw him doing,” the participle agreeing with the object. ἐπὶ τῷ … θολοῦν and … ἐᾶν are articular infinitives naming the ground of the complaint.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἀπεκρίνατο· « Ἀλλ’ ἐὰν μὴ οὕτως ὁ ποταμὸς ταράσσηται, ἐμὲ δεήσει λιμώττοντα ἀποθανεῖν. »
sentences.tr: Ho de apekrinato· « All’ ean mē houtōs ho potamos tarassētai, eme deēsei limōttonta apothanein. »
sentences.l: And he answered: « Well, if the river is not stirred up in this way, it will be necessary for me to die hungering. »
sentences.i: He answered: « If the river is not stirred up like this, I shall have to starve to death. »
sentences.n: ἐὰν μή with the subjunctive (ταράσσηται) and a future in the main clause is the ordinary future condition. δεήσει, the future of δεῖ, takes accusative and infinitive, ἐμέ … ἀποθανεῖν. λιμώττοντα agrees with ἐμέ: Greek says “die hungering” where English says “starve to death.”

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν πόλεων οἱ δημαγωγοὶ τότε μάλιστα ἐνεργάζονται, ὅταν τὰς πατρίδας εἰς στάσεις περιαγάγωσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn poleōn hoi dēmagōgoi tote malista energazontai, hotan tas patridas eis staseis periagagōsin.
sentences.l: So too the demagogues of the cities are then most of all at their work, whenever they have led their fatherlands round into faction.
sentences.i: So too the demagogues in the cities are busiest at their work just when they have brought their own countries round into faction.
sentences.n: The application is political and concrete: στάσις is faction, the civil strife that tore Greek cities apart, and δημαγωγός is literally “leader of the people,” though the fable plainly takes it as an insult. ἐνεργάζονται is awkward here: the verb usually means “produce in, work into” something, and with no object its force is a guess — “are at their work,” or perhaps “make their profit.” ὅταν with the aorist subjunctive (περιαγάγωσιν) gives the general case.
